### Event-triggered and time-triggered bus architectures {#sec-nervous-fieldbus-architectures}

Command transport contributes to the blocking and interference terms in response-time analysis. Two mechanisms produce different timing obligations. On an event-triggered bus, a node requests transmission when it has data, then competes with other traffic. On a time-triggered bus, a configured schedule reserves access in advance. Neither mechanism supplies a complete response bound without assumptions about payloads, competing traffic, faults, and device processing.

Controller Area Network (CAN) and its Flexible Data-Rate variant (CAN-FD) resolve simultaneous requests by message priority. A higher-priority frame wins arbitration, but it still waits for a frame already in progress to finish. Increasing the data bitrate shortens serialization; it does not remove this non-preemptive blocking. The response budget must include both the bytes sent and the longest permitted wait for access.

EtherCAT instead lets a coordinator send a frame that passes through the drives, whose interface hardware reads commands and inserts feedback as the frame passes. A schedule avoids competition among those drives for transmission, while hardware clock synchronization aligns their local updates. Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN) reserves transmission windows on configured Ethernet switches. Its bound depends on the gate schedule, clock error, and traffic admitted to the network. @Sec-appendix-systems-fieldbus supplies the protocol mechanisms and response-time models for evaluating a concrete configuration.

For the mobile manipulator, the design decision is whether the drive commands and feedback fit the allocated bus cycle with enough time left for controller and device response. High-throughput camera links and supervisory middleware need their own budgets, but they must not introduce an unbounded wait into this path. The real-time controller and modular interfaces in @fig-industrial-ethercat-controller illustrate how command coordination can remain local to the drives.

::: {#fig-industrial-ethercat-controller fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Real-time distributed controller with modular I/O**: Dedicated embedded real-time controller and adjacent hardware I/O modules. The unit acts as a deterministic bus coordinator, synchronizing distributed sensor acquisition and motor drive terminals via hardware-scheduled Ethernet telegrams. (Photo: Oleg Yunakov, [Wikimedia Commons](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Beckhoff_IoT_controller_CX5120.jpg), CC BY-SA 4.0)." fig-alt="Photograph of an embedded real-time controller with Ethernet ports and modular I/O terminals."}
![](images/jpg/fig04_real_industrial_ethercat_controller.jpg){width="85%"}
:::

Clock synchronization aligns the instants at which distributed drives sample or update;[^fn-hw-ethercat-dc] it does not measure how long a newly issued command takes to reach them. A tightly aligned set of clocks can still apply an old command if its delivery was delayed. Both command response time and update alignment therefore need explicit bounds.

[^fn-hw-ethercat-dc]: **Distributed Clock**\index{Distributed clock}\index{Time-to-digital converter!timestamp synchrony}: Under IEC 61158-4-12, EtherCAT Distributed Clocks (DC) synchronize distributed servo drive nodes to a reference clock timebase by measuring physical propagation delays across the ring topology. Dedicated Time-to-Digital Converter (TDC) units in each peripheral node controller latch arrival timestamps at physical transceiver pins when the Start of Frame Delimiter (SFD) traverses the port, allowing the bus coordinator to evaluate bidirectional delays ($t_{\text{prop}}$) and discipline local timers so that hardware `SYNC0` pulses fire simultaneously across all joint inverters within $\le 50\text{ ns}$. Clock alignment alone does not bound the complete control cycle, which must also account for controller response time and PWM gate update latency.

### Protocol schedulability comparison between CAN-FD and EtherCAT {#sec-nervous-schedulability-analysis}

On the mobile manipulator the candidate communication links sort strictly by hierarchy:

1. **Board-Level Peripheral Interconnects (SPI, Memory-Mapped I/O):** Connects microcontrollers directly to joint encoders, current-shunt ADCs, and gate drivers with sub-microsecond latency ($< 1\,\mu\text{s}$) under a fixed transfer schedule.
2. **Deterministic Drive Command Buses (EtherCAT, TSN Ethernet):** Transports cyclic joint setpoints and sensor feedback across all distributed drive inverters within an allocated $1.0\text{ ms}$ bus cycle ($T_{\text{bus}}$) with sub-microsecond synchronization jitter ($\sigma_{\text{jitter}} < 100\text{ ns}$).
3. **Chassis and Auxiliary Diagnostic Buses (CAN-FD):** Manages lower-rate battery management systems (BMS), environmental sensors, and diagnostic telemetry where priority arbitration is acceptable under verified worst-case bus load.

None of these bounds belongs to a protocol acronym alone. Each depends on the configured devices, wiring, payload sizes, and schedule. The critical architectural question is whether all servo axes fit within the permission path's bus cycle budget.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-fieldbus-schedulability
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ FIELDBUS SERIALIZATION OCCUPANCY: CAN FD VS. ETHERCAT (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-nervous-fieldbus-serialization-latency-wcet-schedulability,
# │          @fig-04-fieldbus-evolution, and the margin figure.
# │ Goal:    Quantify bus occupancy for the running machine's servo axes with
# │          command AND feedback frames; full response time needs more terms.
# │ Show:    CAN FD frame (8 B, worst-case stuffing) 56.6 us = 34 bits at
# │          1 Mbps + 113 bits at 5 Mbps; one bus, 18 frames = 1018.8 us > 1 ms;
# │          one bus per limb: arm 14 frames = 792.4 us, base 4 frames =
# │          226.4 us; EtherCAT one frame (16 B/axis) + 9 hops = 22.0 us.
# │ How:     calc_canfd_bus_utilization (ISO 11898-1:2015 frame bits) and
# │          calc_ethercat_cycle_time; axis counts and cycle from RM; PDO
# │          sizes and bit rates are scenario inputs.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_latency, fmt_percent, fmt_int, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class FieldbusSchedulability:
    """Scenario serialization and forwarding occupancy, not end-to-end schedulability."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    num_axes = RM.servo_axes  # category: chosen (arm joints + drive wheels)
    arm_axes = RM.arm.dofs  # category: datasheet
    cycle_time = RM.fieldbus_cycle  # category: illustrative (EtherCAT cycle, T_bus)

    # Frame parameters below are scenario assumptions (chosen for this comparison)
    pdo_bytes = 8  # category: chosen (position-mode record: 32-bit position + two 16-bit words, each direction)
    frames_per_axis = 2  # category: chosen (one command frame and one feedback frame per axis per cycle)
    canfd_baud_arb = 1.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: chosen (nominal rate)
    canfd_baud_data = 5.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: chosen (data-phase rate)
    ethercat_baud = 100.0 * (megabit / second)  # category: datasheet (100BASE-TX link rate)
    ethercat_header = 64  # category: illustrative
    ethercat_hop = 0.6 * microsecond  # category: illustrative

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    drive_axes = num_axes - arm_axes
    canfd_kw = dict(
        payload_bytes=pdo_bytes,
        baud_arbitration=canfd_baud_arb,
        baud_data=canfd_baud_data,
        cycle_time=cycle_time,
        frames_per_axis=frames_per_axis,
    )
    one_bus = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(num_axes=num_axes, **canfd_kw)
    arm_bus = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(num_axes=arm_axes, **canfd_kw)
    base_bus = calc_canfd_bus_utilization(num_axes=drive_axes, **canfd_kw)
    ethercat = calc_ethercat_cycle_time(
        num_axes=num_axes,
        bytes_per_axis=frames_per_axis * pdo_bytes,  # command and feedback share one frame
        baud_rate=ethercat_baud,
        header_bytes=ethercat_header,
        hop_delay=ethercat_hop,
        cycle_time=cycle_time,
    )

    t_frame = one_bus["t_tx"]
    t_nom = one_bus["t_nominal"]
    t_dat = one_bus["t_data"]
    bits_nom = one_bus["bits_nominal"]
    bits_dat = one_bus["bits_data"]
    stuff_bits = one_bus["stuff_bits_nominal"] + one_bus["stuff_bits_data"]
    n_frames = one_bus["n_frames"]
    t_total_one = one_bus["t_total_tx"]
    rho_one = one_bus["utilization"]
    n_frames_arm = arm_bus["n_frames"]
    t_total_arm = arm_bus["t_total_tx"]
    rho_arm = arm_bus["utilization"]
    t_left_arm = (cycle_time - t_total_arm).to(microsecond)
    n_frames_base = base_bus["n_frames"]
    t_total_base = base_bus["t_total_tx"]
    rho_base = base_bus["utilization"]

    t_frame_ethercat = ethercat["t_tx"]
    t_hop_ethercat = ethercat["t_forward"]
    t_total_ethercat = ethercat["t_cycle_total"]
    t_margin_ethercat = ethercat["t_margin"]
    rho_ethercat = ethercat["utilization"]

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    # 2026-09-28 (M1): command AND feedback frames, CRC and stuffing in the data
    # phase, 8-byte records; replaces the 9-frame, 64-byte, CRC-at-nominal model.
    check(num_axes == 9 and arm_axes == 7 and drive_axes == 2, f"Axis split drifted: {num_axes} = {arm_axes} + {drive_axes}")
    check(abs(cycle_time.to(millisecond).magnitude - 1.0) < 1e-9, f"Bus cycle drifted: {cycle_time}")
    check(bits_nom == 34 and bits_dat == 113, f"CAN FD frame bits drifted: {bits_nom} + {bits_dat}")
    check(abs(t_frame.to(microsecond).magnitude - 56.6) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected CAN FD frame time: {t_frame}")
    check(abs(t_total_one.to(microsecond).magnitude - 1018.8) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected single-bus total: {t_total_one}")
    check(rho_one > 1.0, "One CAN FD bus for nine axes must overrun the 1 ms cycle")
    check(abs(t_total_arm.to(microsecond).magnitude - 792.4) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected arm-bus total: {t_total_arm}")
    check(abs(t_total_base.to(microsecond).magnitude - 226.4) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected base-bus total: {t_total_base}")
    check(rho_arm < 1.0 and rho_base < 1.0, "Per-limb buses must pass the serialization check")
    check(abs(t_total_ethercat.to(microsecond).magnitude - 22.04) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected EtherCAT total: {t_total_ethercat}")
    check(abs(t_margin_ethercat.to(microsecond).magnitude - 977.96) < 1e-6, f"Unexpected unallocated bus time: {t_margin_ethercat}")
    check(rho_ethercat < 0.05, "EtherCAT utilization must be under 5%")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    num_axes_str = fmt_int(num_axes)
    arm_axes_str = fmt_int(arm_axes)
    drive_axes_str = fmt_int(drive_axes)
    cycle_time_str = fmt_latency(cycle_time, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    pdo_bytes_str = fmt_int(pdo_bytes)
    ethercat_pdo_str = fmt_int(frames_per_axis * pdo_bytes)

    bits_nom_str = fmt_int(bits_nom)
    bits_dat_str = fmt_int(bits_dat)
    stuff_bits_str = fmt_int(stuff_bits)
    t_nom_str = fmt_latency(t_nom, unit=microsecond, precision=0)
    t_dat_str = fmt_latency(t_dat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_frame_str = fmt_latency(t_frame, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    n_frames_str = fmt_int(n_frames)
    t_total_one_str = fmt_latency(t_total_one, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_one_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_one, precision=1, style="prose")
    n_frames_arm_str = fmt_int(n_frames_arm)
    t_total_arm_str = fmt_latency(t_total_arm, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_arm_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_arm, precision=1, style="prose")
    t_left_arm_str = fmt_latency(t_left_arm, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    n_frames_base_str = fmt_int(n_frames_base)
    t_total_base_str = fmt_latency(t_total_base, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_base_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_base, precision=1, style="prose")

    t_frame_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_frame_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_hop_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_hop_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_total_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_total_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    t_margin_ethercat_str = fmt_latency(t_margin_ethercat, unit=microsecond, precision=1)
    rho_ethercat_pct_str = fmt_percent(rho_ethercat, precision=1, style="prose")
```

::: {#nbk-nervous-fieldbus-serialization-latency-wcet-schedulability .callout-notebook title="Fieldbus serialization before schedulability"}
**Practical engineering question**: The mobile manipulator's permission path exchanges position setpoints and feedback with `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` servo axes, `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.arm_axes_str` arm joints and `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.drive_axes_str` drive wheels, once per `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time_str` bus cycle. Each direction carries an `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.pdo_bytes_str`-byte record per axis, a 32-bit position and two 16-bit words (a scenario choice). How much of that cycle do the CAN FD frames or one EtherCAT frame occupy before controller and device delays are counted?

*1. CAN FD serialization (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.pdo_bytes_str`-byte frames, $1.0\text{ Mbps}$ nominal, $5.0\text{ Mbps}$ data):*

- A CAN frame carries one message, so each axis needs a command frame and a feedback frame, `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.n_frames_str` frames per cycle for all axes.
- Only the arbitration bits before the bit-rate switch and the delimiter, acknowledgment, end-of-frame, and intermission bits after it run at the nominal rate: `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.bits_nom_str` bits, or `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_nom_str`. The data-length code, the payload, the stuff count, the 17-bit CRC, and the CRC's fixed stuff bits run at the data rate [@iso11898-1-2015; @bosch2012canfd]: `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.bits_dat_str` bits, or `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_dat_str`.
- Both counts include the worst-case dynamic stuff bits (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.stuff_bits_str` for this frame), because a response bound must assume the bit pattern that lengthens the frame most.
- One frame therefore takes `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_frame_str`, and `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.n_frames_str` frames on one bus take `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_one_str`, or `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_one_pct_str` of the cycle, before any other delay is counted.
- The usual remedy splits the axes across parallel buses, one per limb. The arm's `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.n_frames_arm_str` frames then take `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_arm_str` (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_arm_pct_str`), and the base's `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.n_frames_base_str` frames take `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_base_str` (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_base_pct_str`). The arm bus passes this necessary check with `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_left_arm_str` left for non-preemptive blocking, competing frames, error retransmissions, and response-time analysis; no universal utilization threshold establishes schedulability.

*2. EtherCAT on-the-fly processing (`{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` axes, daisy-chain ring):*

- Bitrate: $100\text{ Mbps}$ full-duplex Fast Ethernet ($10\text{ ns/bit}$).
- A single Ethernet frame carries every axis's command and feedback, `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.ethercat_pdo_str` bytes per axis, in one pass.
- Frame serialization time: `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_frame_ethercat_str`.
- Hardware forwarding mechanism: Dedicated EtherCAT peripheral node controller application-specific integrated circuits (ASICs) (such as the Beckhoff ET1100) utilize internal hardware shift registers to extract commanded setpoints and insert sensor feedback on the fly as the physical Ethernet telegram traverses the node. Because the frame is never stored in a software buffer before retransmission, each physical peripheral node introduces only an internal silicon gate delay ($0.6\,\mu\text{s}$ per hop).
- Node forwarding delay: `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` peripheral ASIC controller hops at $0.6\,\mu\text{s}$ per hop $=$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_hop_ethercat_str`.
- Modeled frame serialization plus `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` forwarding hops: $T_{\text{occupancy}} =$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_frame_ethercat_str` $+$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_hop_ethercat_str` $=$ `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_total_ethercat_str`.
- Result: These modeled bus terms occupy `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.rho_ethercat_pct_str` of the cycle, leaving `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_margin_ethercat_str` **unallocated by this bus calculation**. Coordinator/node processing, propagation, clock synchronization, retries, application computation, and actuator response still consume the end-to-end deadline.

**Systems insight**: CAN FD's fast data phase does not rescue a single bus, because every frame still pays its arbitration and trailer bits at the nominal rate and CAN needs two frames per axis where EtherCAT needs one frame for all of them. For this scenario's `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.num_axes_str` axes, one CAN FD bus misses the `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.cycle_time_str` cycle on serialization alone; a bus per limb fits, with the arm bus heavily loaded. EtherCAT frame and forwarding occupancy leaves `{python} FieldbusSchedulability.t_margin_ethercat_str` for the remaining work. Neither calculation proves the complete response bound. Arbitration, blocking, and retransmission allowances belong in the CAN FD analysis; coordinator, device, and fault-response delays belong in the EtherCAT analysis. Each additional transport delay consumes stopping clearance as $v \cdot \Delta t_{\text{bus}}$.
:::

### Bandwidth and jitter trade-offs on the synchronization frontier {#sec-nervous-synchronization-frontier}

The serialization example separates three quantities that a bus specification can otherwise blur. Bandwidth bounds how many bytes fit in an interval. Command response time includes waiting, transmission, and processing before a drive can act. Synchronization jitter bounds variation in the relative timing of distributed updates. A design can improve one while leaving another unchanged.

The configured scenario in @fig-04-fieldbus-evolution compares only serialization and forwarding occupancy against the allocated bus cycle. It rejects a single CAN FD bus for all nine axes before a full response analysis and leaves the per-limb buses and EtherCAT to be evaluated. It supplies neither a synchronization-jitter bound nor a complete response bound. A CAN-FD schedule needs a bound on competing frames and non-preemptive blocking; an EtherCAT path needs frame, forwarding, and device delays; a TSN schedule needs reserved windows and clock-error allowances.[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus] These are inputs to the response calculation, not guarantees obtained by selecting a protocol name.

Freshness adds a further requirement. Even a command delivered within its transport bound may have been computed from old evidence. The proposal header's evidence timestamp and expiry therefore remain necessary on a synchronized network. The transport budget must leave room for the command's physical response, and the permission path must refuse a command whose authority has ended.

[^fn-net-tsn-fieldbus]: **Time-Sensitive Networking**\index{Time-sensitive networking}: IEEE 802.1Qbv Time-Sensitive Networking establishes deterministic Ethernet communication by configuring time-aware traffic shapers across network switches. High-priority control frames execute within dedicated, pre-scheduled transmission windows, while asynchronous high-bandwidth payloads (such as uncompressed camera streams) are temporarily gated. A bounded path delivers each command to the drives within its cycle, but it is indifferent to which commands it carries. Which processor may place a command on that path, and what that processor must check first, is a question of authority rather than timing.

## Actuation Authority {#sec-nervous-actuation-authority}

A mailbox cannot protect the mobile manipulator if the host also has a diagnostic route that writes directly to a drive. The partition established in @sec-nervous-silicon-partitioning therefore needs exclusive control over every path that can energize the windings. Actuation authority is this physical ability to change drive commands, including PWM registers, current references, and bridge-enable signals. The host publishes proposals; the permission path alone admits commands to those interfaces (@fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers).

::: {#fig-04-privilege-enforcer-registers fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Hardware proposal boundary**: (a) Decoupled enforcer on an isolated safety microcontroller with exclusive write privilege over motor drive registers, while the host processor proposes trajectories across a board-level link into the microcontroller's own memory. (b) Collapsed unsafe architecture where unverified host software writes actuator registers directly, creating a single failure domain." fig-alt="Comparison of hardware privilege architectures: (a) Decoupled real-time enforcer gating actuator registers with a separate torque-cutoff trip branch; (b) Unsafe collapsed architecture with direct unchecked writes from host to motor registers."}
![](images/svg/fig04_privilege_enforcer_registers.svg){width="90%"}
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Actuator override masking registers implement the hardware preemption tiers formulated in @sec-intervention-authority-log.
:::

The microcontroller continuously evaluates physical safety invariants: verifying that commanded joint positions lie within physical reach envelopes, that joint velocities do not exceed certified limits, and that projected decelerations remain safely within dynamic stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$). If a proposal satisfies all invariants, the microcontroller grants execution permission and interpolates waypoints into position setpoints for each bus cycle, which the drives execute through their own velocity and current loops. An invalid or expired candidate is refused ($\bot$); it does not automatically revoke a different active chunk. The active chunk continues only while its own state, evidence, and lease remain valid. When those checks fail, the enforcer ends its authority and requests a controlled deceleration or hold. A separate hardware trip zone can remove drive torque on a fault; opening switches does not itself brake moving mass.[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]

[^fn-hw-tripzone-break]: **Hardware Trip Zone**\index{Hardware trip zone}: Microcontroller hardware trip zones (such as TI `EPWM_TZFRC` or STM32 `TIMx_BDTR` Break inputs) couple analog overcurrent and overvoltage comparators directly to timer output logic. Upon fault detection, configured trip logic may force gate signals high-impedance or activate a validated braking mode. These have different mechanical consequences: torque removal can leave the plant coasting, while dynamic braking requires a rated energy path.

Controlled stopping and torque removal impose different obligations. Powered braking uses the drives to remove motion before torque is disabled; immediate torque removal can leave a base coasting or a loaded arm falling. Holding position requires continued torque or a separately rated restraint. The stop-category comparison in @sec-enforcement-stop-categories develops these alternatives. At this interface, the requirement is to specify the physical response and reserve the time and energy it needs.

The refusal carries its own physical cost. If the enforcer rejects an invalid proposal and commands dynamic braking on a fast-moving joint, the braking path must have enough torque, clearance, and thermal capacity to arrest the mass.[^fn-math-braking-dynamics] Over a braking interval of hundreds of milliseconds, the winding resistance, brake resistor, or friction that forms that path must absorb the joint's kinetic energy within the thermal limits of @sec-body-thermal-duty-cycles, without damaging the winding insulation or letting the mass coast past its clearance.

[^fn-math-braking-dynamics]: **Braking Dynamics**\index{Braking dynamics}: Arresting a high-inertia manipulator joint transfers kinetic energy into the implemented braking path: winding and power electronics losses, a rated brake resistor, or mechanical friction. The trajectory must satisfy stopping clearance ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) and each component's pulse-energy and thermal limits; $\int I^2R\,dt$ accounts for the winding share when resistive motor braking is used. The stopping-distance derivation is in @sec-appendix-systems-stopping; @sec-appendix-systems-actuators develops the winding-heating and thermal-limit models.

By virtue of the causal boundary established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, the enforcer treats the origin of an aberrant proposal as irrelevant. A remote memory exploit in an operating system daemon, an adversarial camera perturbation inducing model hallucination, and an arithmetic overflow in a neural matrix multiplier all produce the same boundary event, an invalid proposal packet. Because the enforcer evaluates invariant bounds against physical sensor feedback from optical encoders and current shunts rather than inspecting neural network weights, it needs no model of why a proposal went wrong, and the host, which cannot write actuator registers directly, has no path around it. Protection against a compromised host still depends on independent sensing, a correct limit model, actuator capability, and a feasible fallback.

If the enforcer itself hangs, it may be unable to request that controlled response. An out-of-band interlock must then trigger the separately qualified fault response. Safe Torque Off (STO) prevents torque-producing drive signals; it does not isolate the main supply or guarantee that a moving load stops within the normal powered-braking budget.[^fn-std-iec61800-sto] A separate contactor can provide supply isolation, and a rated brake or other restraint may be needed to contain the resulting motion. The illustrated interlock (@fig-real-estop) makes the torque-inhibit path independent of the proposal software; qualification must still establish its behavior under shared power, clock, and wiring faults.

[^fn-std-iec61800-sto]: **Safe Torque Off (STO)**\index{Safe torque off}: An STO implementation removes torque-producing drive signals through a hardware interlock. An IEC 61800-5-2 integrity rating depends on the actual devices, diagnostic coverage, wiring, and validation, not on the circuit pattern alone.

::: {#fig-real-estop fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Illustrative out-of-band interlock and STO path**: A dual-channel emergency switch and monitored relays remove torque-producing gate bias; a separate spring-applied holding brake is shown. This diagram describes a hardware response path, not a certified integrity level or proof of stopping distance (synthesized from ISO 13849-1 and IEC 61800-5-2)." fig-alt="Four-stage out-of-band safety interlock schematic: Dual-channel positive-break E-stop, force-guided safety relays with EDM feedback, gate bias cutoff with holding brake, and motor plant de-energized to zero torque."}
![](images/svg/fig04_sto_safety_circuit.svg){width="100%"}
:::

The switch and monitored relay channels detect an emergency input or channel disagreement and inhibit drive torque. The spring-applied holding brake provides a separate restraint. Its name does not establish a dynamic stopping capability: normal powered deceleration applies it after rest, while emergency application during motion needs its own energy and stopping-distance qualification. The response selection and sequencing in @sec-enforcement-stop-categories depend on those physical capabilities.

::: {#psp-nervous-hardware-authority .callout-perspective title="Hardware authority invariant"}
If an unverified learned policy has direct memory-mapped write access to actuator gate-driver registers, the machine has no safety layer, and its next out-of-distribution input reaches the motors unchecked.
:::

Write privilege is therefore a physical fact about wires and registers, not a software permission, and the Brain holds none of it. That privilege protects the plant only while the enforcer stays independent of the processor whose proposals it refuses. If the two share a clock, a rail, or a memory bus, a fault in the proposer can silence the enforcer without ever writing to a drive.

## Hardware Isolation {#sec-nervous-hardware-isolation}

A separate permission processor can still reset when an accelerator burst pulls down their shared supply. It can also miss a tick while waiting for a shared memory bus. The partition therefore needs evidence about common resources, not another software boundary. Execution, timing, power, and memory define the fault paths that must be examined.

Private execution resources, independent timing references, isolated power rails, and bounded memory access can contain these paths.[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi] Where resources remain shared, the design must show that interference and the declared common-cause faults cannot defeat the permission deadline or its qualified fallback. @Sec-placement develops the resource allocation and loaded measurements for that decision; here the obligation is to carry each dependency into the Transport Budget.

[^fn-std-iso26262-ffi]: **Freedom from Interference (FFI)**\index{Freedom from interference}: ISO 26262-9 and IEC 61508 formalize Freedom from Interference (FFI) as the absence of cascading faults between software elements possessing different safety integrity levels. Unverified neural policies sharing silicon or bus fabrics with safety-critical tasks require architects to demonstrate spatial (memory protection), temporal (independent scheduling and timers), and electrical isolation (independent power rails). Shared resources require evidence that interference cannot defeat the specified enforcement deadlines and fault response.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-permission-rail
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ SHARED CONTROL RAIL VS. THE HELD-UP PERMISSION RAIL (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation, the shared-infrastructure paragraph.
# │ Goal:    Name the rail the application processor shares and the isolated,
# │          held-up rail the permission path runs on instead.
# │ Show:    24 V shared control rail, 18 V regulator dropout, 2 s hold-up.
# │ How:     Registry fields on RM; the sag below the dropout is derived in
# │          @sec-body-power-integrity, and the hold-up is sized in
# │          @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_voltage, fmt_latency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator

class PermissionRail:
    """The permission path's isolated, held-up rail beside the shared control rail."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v_rail = RM.control_rail_nominal  # category: chosen (shared 24 V control rail)
    v_dropout = RM.control_rail_dropout  # category: illustrative (regulator dropout)
    t_holdup = RM.permission_rail_holdup  # category: chosen (permission-rail hold-up)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    v_headroom = (v_rail - v_dropout).to(volt)  # headroom a full-charge rail starts with

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(v_rail.to(volt).magnitude - 24.0) < 1e-9, f"Control rail drifted: {v_rail}")
    check(abs(v_dropout.to(volt).magnitude - 18.0) < 1e-9, f"Regulator dropout drifted: {v_dropout}")
    check(abs(t_holdup.to(second).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Permission-rail hold-up drifted: {t_holdup}")
    check(v_headroom.magnitude > 0, "The shared rail must start above its regulator dropout")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_rail_str = fmt_voltage(v_rail, unit=volt, precision=0)
    v_dropout_str = fmt_voltage(v_dropout, unit=volt, precision=0)
    t_holdup_str = fmt_latency(t_holdup, unit=second, precision=0)
```

Shared electrical and physical infrastructure creates cross-domain failure modes that bypass all software access controls. On the mobile manipulator, the application processor and the permission path share a primary battery but not a power rail. When drive motors accelerate under peak torque or GPU accelerators launch sudden inference bursts, transient current draws can sag the shared `{python} PermissionRail.v_rail_str` control rail below its regulators' `{python} PermissionRail.v_dropout_str` dropout threshold (@sec-body-power-integrity), causing unisolated processors to brown out and reset. If the safety microcontroller shared that unisolated rail, a brownout would float its GPIO lines to high impedance during reboot; floating gate-driver pins risk destructive shoot-through across inverter MOSFETs or leave the machine's moving kinetic momentum ($E_k = \frac{1}{2} m v^2$) coasting uncontrolled through clearance. To keep the permission path available during this transient, it runs on the isolated rail of @sec-body-archetype-matrix, held up with diode-isolated storage capacitors for `{python} PermissionRail.t_holdup_str`. While the application processor reboots, the held-up rail lets the safety microcontroller receive the undervoltage flag and request a fallback. Continued logic power does not guarantee braking power or torque. A controlled stop still requires sufficient drive power, braking capability, and clearance; if those are unavailable, the design needs a qualified unpowered response whose brake engagement and resulting motion fit the physical budget.

On a shared silicon package or common thermal heat sink, sustained computational load on the application processor elevates junction temperatures beyond $105^\circ\text{C}$, triggering thermal throttling or silicon shutdown in adjacent real-time cores. When communication relies on an arbitrated interface such as a shared peripheral interconnect or memory bus, a high-bandwidth visual pipeline or a misbehaving direct memory access controller can saturate bus bandwidth, starving the permission path of encoder feedback and sensor telemetry. Even a common clock oscillator creates an unbudgeted single point of failure, where thermal drift, mechanical vibration, or crystal cracking desynchronizes both domains at the same instant.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_substrate_blast_radius.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="Blast radius diagram showing a compute and drive transient sagging the shared control rail, with thermal coupling, DMA starvation, and clock jitter spreading across a shared substrate, and the sag stopping at the isolated, held-up permission rail."}

*A transient on the shared rail reaches every load that draws from it; the permission path rides through on its own isolated, held-up rail.*
:::

The permission path must distinguish two failure modes of the proposer, unresponsiveness and corruption. Unresponsiveness occurs when an inference pipeline hangs, a scheduling deadline is missed, or operating system memory fragmentation blocks execution, producing no output. A host failure can trip the heartbeat timer; a live host that stops publishing admissible chunks instead reaches the active chunk's lease or evidence deadline. These are the distinct timer obligations established in @sec-nervous-supervisory-timers.

Corruption occurs when the proposer remains fully active and passes its heartbeat deadline, but generates kinematically impossible setpoints, discontinuous velocity requests, or numerical infinities resulting from out-of-distribution visual inputs or matrix overflow. The enforcer answers the two failures through separate mechanisms. A missing fresh chunk or a missed heartbeat revokes the proposal when its timer expires, whereas corruption triggers an immediate invariant rejection on the arrival of the malformed proposal packet.

The timer distinction now has a physical consequence. A live heartbeat cannot justify continued tracking after the active chunk expires; the stopping-budget lease ends that authority independently.[^fn-math-watchdog-lease] The coupled budget in @sec-nervous-coupled-budget checks whether the chunk policy can supply renewals often enough. It also shows why the slower intent model must supply goals rather than hold the motion lease itself.

[^fn-math-watchdog-lease]: **Chunk Lease Bound**\index{Watchdog lease!bound}: For a constant-speed approach, the chunk lease, the tick, the bus cycle, and brake onset must satisfy the pre-brake inequality of @sec-nervous-cadences once the observation age $t_{\text{age}}$ joins them on the left side, and a post-expiry hold $T_{\text{hold}}$ adds to that side as well. The right-hand side is the pre-brake ceiling, not a lease to spend in full. For the complete algebraic derivation of lease bounds under bounded deceleration, see @sec-appendix-control-teleop-leases.

A timer feed proves only that the feed path ran. In *Bookout v. Toyota* (2013), a plaintiff expert argued that a timer-tick interrupt kept servicing the watchdog while other tasks could die [@barr2013toyota]; this was an argument made in litigation, not a technical finding, and the NASA and NHTSA investigation identified no electronic cause of large unintended accelerations [@nasa2011toyota].

When active authority ends and no admissible continuation remains, the permission path executes an explicit degradation strategy rather than an unconditioned power cut, because cutting power hands a moving actuator to whichever unpowered state its drive falls into (@sec-body-power-integrity), and none of those states is a controlled stop. The permission path selects degradation from the current physical state and the responses still feasible there. An optional short continuation of the last validated trajectory is permissible only while its state, evidence, chunk lease, and stopping margin remain valid. After expiry, any separately authorized fallback delay $T_{\text{hold}}$ enters $\tau_{\text{delay}}$ and must fit in the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_left_str` of pre-brake ceiling that the lease path and brake onset leave at the drive limit (\ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}); the enforcer must begin braking sooner if the measured bounds of the remaining terms do not fit. The permission path requests controlled deceleration before that budget is exhausted using the available torque and thermal budget established in @sec-body-actuator-limits. It reaches rest only if clearance and braking capability remain sufficient. A gravity-loaded arm may require a rated mechanical holding brake after motion has been arrested.

Once the physical plant is brought to a complete, stationary halt, the architecture executes a **recovery handshake**\index{Recovery handshake} before restoring autonomous proposal authority. The safety microcontroller asserts a persistent `FAULT_HELD` latch in a status word it owns and reports the exact physical rest pose $(\mathbf{q}_{\text{rest}}, \dot{\mathbf{q}} = \mathbf{0})$. The application processor must discard stale action chunks, invalidate state tied to the interrupted motion, ingest fresh observations tagged with new hardware timestamps, and publish a re-synchronized chunk proposal.

Recovery must also invalidate proposal-side state that assumes the pre-fault motion continued. For an autoregressive policy, this can include cached tokens or a key-value (KV) attention cache; the required reset depends on what the model stores and how it incorporates fresh observations. A cache flush alone does not establish physical continuity. The microcontroller verifies that the initial waypoint of the new proposal matches the physical rest state within a strict spatial epsilon ($||\mathbf{a}_0 - \mathbf{q}_{\text{rest}}|| \le \epsilon_{\text{sync}}$) before releasing the fault latch and restoring proposal authority.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Real-time bus fault-recovery state machines are verified via hardware fault-injection in @sec-verification-hardware-fault-injection.
:::

Verifying that these isolation boundaries function as designed requires physical falsification on the test bench. Four specific fault-injection regimes must be executed against the physical prototype: power-rail droop testing (injecting maximum-slew current steps to verify less than $50\text{ mV}$ of rail cross-coupling noise), clock glitching (verifying independent timing domains maintain stable cycle counts under frequency drift), communication bus flooding (saturating links to verify heartbeat telemetry retains deterministic transmission slots),[^fn-hw-canfd-arbitration] and numerical fault injection (streaming synthetic proposals containing NaNs and infinite floats to verify single-cycle rejection without execution stalls).

[^fn-hw-canfd-arbitration]: **CAN Arbitration**\index{CAN arbitration}: Controller Area Network protocols resolve bus contention at the physical layer using wired-AND dominant ('0') and recessive ('1') signaling. If a defective transceiver continuously asserts a dominant state (a "babbling idiot" fault), it monopolizes the shared physical bus and blocks all higher-level communication. Hardware bus guardians and dominant-timeout clamp circuits monitor transmission duration, physically disconnecting jabbering nodes to preserve network availability for remaining safety participants.

Independence is therefore validated against identified common-cause faults rather than read off a block diagram, and the lease that bounds a stopped proposer comes from the stopping margin that remains after detection and actuation delays. Both defenses bound a proposer that stops or fails, which leaves open whether a proposer running at the enforcer's own rate still needs a separate check.

## Invariant Checking {#sec-nervous-invariant-checking}

Locomotion policies and compact visuomotor models compiled for edge accelerators can emit a new actuator command every $2.0\text{ ms}$, which tempts designers to let the policy write the motor registers directly. Rate matching does not confer authority. A neural network emitting torques at $500\text{ Hz}$ is governed by the same statistical uncertainty as a large model generating waypoints at $5\text{ Hz}$, and even when policy and enforcer share one $2.0\text{ ms}$ period, the network's output remains a proposal that must pass the proposal boundary of @sec-boundary-machine-model before it changes current in a winding.

Placing an unverified policy inside the fast loop exposes the plant to three classical systems failure modes:

1. *Compute underrun:* Occurs when tail latency jitter pushes an inference pass beyond the actuation deadline ($t_{\text{infer}} > D_i$), leaving the motor inverter without a fresh setpoint unless a deterministic default is latched.
2. *Out-of-distribution torque spikes:* Occurs when an adversarial visual input or unseen physical contact state produces an instantaneous, discontinuous torque reversal within a single cycle.
3. *Structural limit cycling:* Occurs when unmodeled gearbox compliance or sensor phase lag couples with high-gain neural policy feedback into self-excited limit-cycle resonance.

The interface must reject an inadmissible candidate without waiting for the producer, and recheck the active command against current physical state. Position and velocity limits ($\mathbf{q} \in [\mathbf{q}_{\min}, \mathbf{q}_{\max}]$ and $|\dot{\mathbf{q}}| \le \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\max}$) are necessary but do not by themselves establish a feasible stop. A torque-slew constraint, $|\dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}| = |(\boldsymbol{\tau}_k - \boldsymbol{\tau}_{k-1})/\Delta t| \le \dot{\boldsymbol{\tau}}_{\max}$, can limit command changes, but a corrected command must still satisfy the other physical limits. Contact may additionally require accounting for exchanged energy, $\int \boldsymbol{\tau}^T \dot{\mathbf{q}}\,dt$; @sec-appendix-control-passivity develops that background.

Choosing and composing those filters requires the state and motion models developed later in the volume. @Sec-enforcement constructs the admissibility calculation and selects a feasible continuation, hold, or stop. The architectural result here is its execution contract: checks must finish within their allocated response time, use qualified physical evidence, and retain sole actuator authority. Neither fast inference nor a fast rejection routine establishes that contract on its own.

The same reasoning covers the one proposer that is not learned. A remote operator is a third proposer. Its commands pass the same permission path, and network delay spends the same pre-brake budget (@sec-intervention-human-authority). Neither speed nor a human origin gives a proposal authority; only passing the permission path's checks does, and each check spends part of a budget that the next section lays out handoff by handoff.

::: {#chk-nervous-hardware-invariants .callout-checkpoint title="Hardware isolation and invariant checking"}

Before turning to the handoffs between proposer and actuator, verify your understanding of the exchange, hardware isolation, and pre-actuation invariant defenses:

- [ ] **Nonblocking exchange**: Can you explain how the seqlock reader detects a torn read in one bounded attempt, and why a writer stopped mid-write cannot extend the active spline's state, evidence, or lease validity?
- [ ] **Four dimensions of physical isolation**: Can you enumerate the four physical boundaries (silicon pipelines, timing crystals, power rails, memory buses) that a check for fault-domain independence must cover, and explain how shared paths would need validation?
- [ ] **Physical derivation of chunk leases**: Can you explain why the chunk lease must be sized from stopping distance and clearance rather than chosen as a software timeout, and why a heartbeat never renews it?
- [ ] **Rate matching and authority**: Can you explain why a policy that runs at the plant's own rate still produces only proposals, and what timing, state, and fallback obligations remain?

:::

## The Handoffs Matrix {#sec-nervous-handoffs-matrix}

When the mobile manipulator overruns a stop, the diagnosis starts by locating the fault at one of five canonical handoffs between the photons its cameras collect and the current its drives deliver. In distributed systems engineering, microservices communicate across typed interface contracts governed by service-level objectives (SLOs)—such as target $P_{99}$ request latencies, network throughput allocations, and error budgets. In cloud environments, these are soft contracts: when a microservice violates an SLO, the distributed runtime absorbs the error via exponential-backoff retries, request rerouting, circuit breaking, or degraded response modes. In physical AI architectures, however, the five canonical handoffs define **hard cyber-physical service-level objectives**. Because software cannot recall moving kinetic momentum or undo thermal copper heating, an unbudgeted interface violation cannot be masked by software retries.

Upstream, sensing transfers raw transducer signals to perception pipelines. Perception yields intermediate representations that fuse into an estimated world state. The state feeds the learned policy to produce an action plan. The plan submits candidate trajectories to the safety enforcer. Finally, the approved command passes from the enforcer to the physical actuators. Across each boundary, five interface limits govern feasibility: latency ($\tau$), bandwidth ($\beta$), energy and heat ($\mathcal{E}$), determinism ($\sigma_t$), and fault domain isolation ($\mathcal{F}$). The five handoffs and the five interface limits form a five-by-five matrix that maps every signal path to the physical budgets of the machine. The limits are distinct from the body's five budgets of @sec-body-five-budgets, which enter the matrix chiefly through its latency and energy columns. The record this section produces, the **Transport Budget** (formalized on the machine as the **handoff record**\index{Transport budget!contract}\index{Handoff record}), consumes the Limit Record of @sec-body-measuring-limits and the proposer limits established in @sec-brain, including latency, renewal frequency, and evidence age in the same structural format.

The example allocation in @tbl-04-synthesis-grid marks which limits are design-limiting at each handoff, and its numbers are chosen budgets, not measurements. The matrix gathers the budgets of all three Part I chapters, together with the sensor capture that @sec-boundary-machine-model places at the Boundary. In the Boundary row ($\mathcal{H}_1$), where the world becomes measurement, bandwidth and latency bind first, because raw multi-camera pixels stream over SerDes lanes and the exposure window sets a floor on image age before serialization begins. The Brain rows ($\mathcal{H}_2$, $\mathcal{H}_3$) bind first on energy and latency, the inference costs that @sec-brain established. The Body row ($\mathcal{H}_5$) binds first on determinism and heat, because the current loops of @sec-body must run on time and every ampere they deliver warms the windings and the power stage.

The Nervous System row ($\mathcal{H}_4$) is the architectural bridge that ties the Brain and the Body together. The proposal boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model) between the learned planner and the enforcer carries an action proposal ($p_t$), which consists of a compact spline parameterization or waypoint chunk. For the compact payload assumed in this grid, $\beta < 100\text{ kB/s}$ is budgeted, so bandwidth does not bind at this boundary; latency, determinism ($\sigma_t$), and fault domain isolation ($\mathcal{F}$) do. The permission path isolates stochastic proposals with nonblocking mailboxes and expiring leases. On the mobile manipulator the latency limit is the chunk lease, which takes `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` of the `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling at the drive limit (@sec-nervous-cadences), and the active command is rechecked within each `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` permission tick. Full trajectory admission has a separate work and response budget and must finish before a candidate becomes active; the tick does not imply that arbitrary map queries or whole-trajectory validation fit within it. Isolation rests on a private bus, a separate oscillator, and the isolated, held-up rail of @sec-nervous-hardware-isolation.

From the causal boundary perspective framed in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary, an interface failure can be localized to the handoff and budget it violates. Semantic mistakes or missing physical assumptions can still escape an otherwise timely interface; the matrix does not replace task evaluation or hazard analysis. When diagnosing an over-budget stop, trajectory overrun, or subsystem fault, engineers walk @tbl-04-synthesis-grid through a three-step operational root-cause procedure:

1. *Locate the boundary seam:* Identify which physical handoff ($\mathcal{H}_1\text{--}\mathcal{H}_5$) recorded the initial timing excursion, sequence gap, torn payload, or thermal trip.
2. *Check the binding dimension:* Query the specific physical limit ($\tau, \beta, \mathcal{E}, \sigma_t, \mathcal{F}$) designated as *BINDING* for that handoff cell, which dictates the resource bottleneck governing the interface.
3. *Evaluate like-for-like evidence:* Compare runtime diagnostic traces directly against the recorded bound kind (`requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`), verifying whether the failure stemmed from an unmodeled microarchitectural tail event or a physical budget violation.

A handoff diagnosis must compare like evidence. For the $\mathcal{H}_2$ state-estimation path, suppose engineers allocate a $30.0\text{ ms}$ latency budget and measure $P_{99}=24.5\text{ ms}$ on a baseline hardware-in-the-loop run, a sampled margin of $+5.5\text{ ms}$. After thermal throttling, a measured $P_{99}=85.0\text{ ms}$ gives $-55.0\text{ ms}$ against that design budget. The decision is to reduce or reallocate workload and retain independent enforcement while revalidating. A $P_{99}$ sample diagnoses the regression; it is not a worst-case timing proof.

| Canonical Handoff Boundary                                  | Latency Limit ($\tau$)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         | Bandwidth Limit ($\beta$)                                                                                      | Energy & Heat Limit ($\mathcal{E}$)                                                                 | Determinism Limit ($\sigma_t$)                                                                     | Fault Domain Isolation ($\mathcal{F}$)                                                          |
|:------------------------------------------------------------|:-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| **$\mathcal{H}_1$: Sensing $\to$ Perception** *(Boundary)*  | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 16.7\text{ ms}$ (exposure & readout sets sensor age)                                                                                                                                                                                            | **BINDING** \newline $\beta \ge 1.2\text{ GB/s}$ (multi-camera 4K uncompressed streams)                        | *Non-binding* \newline $P < 3\text{ W}$ (sensor head dissipation isolated)                          | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t \le 1.0\text{ ms}$ (frame-sync triggers prevent skew)               | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by SerDes hardware & DMA ring buffers                           |
| **$\mathcal{H}_2$: Perception $\to$ State** *(Brain)*       | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 30.0\text{ ms}$ (visual-inertial odometry & feature window)                                                                                                                                                                                     | *Non-binding* \newline $\beta \approx 10\text{--}50\text{ MB/s}$ (compressed keypoints & voxels)               | **BINDING** \newline $P \approx 15\text{--}35\text{ W}$ (edge vision backbone accelerator envelope) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by sliding-window state estimator buffers                          | **BINDING** \newline Spatial memory isolation: MPUs prevent memory corruption                   |
| **$\mathcal{H}_3$: State $\to$ Plan** *(Brain)*             | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 100.0\text{ ms}$ (autoregressive tokenization & diffusion horizon)                                                                                                                                                                              | *Non-binding* \newline $\beta < 5\text{ MB/s}$ (low-dimensional state & prompt embeddings)                     | **BINDING** \newline $P \approx 30\text{--}75\text{ W}$ (transformer/diffusion matrix accelerators) | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by receding-horizon chunking & spline buffers                      | **BINDING** \newline Host faults must not halt the independent permission path                  |
| **$\mathcal{H}_4$: Plan $\to$ Enforcer** *(Nervous System)* | **BINDING** \newline chunk lease `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_lease_str` (candidate allocation; complete age-to-admission budget still required); active-command checks within each `{python} MachineLeaseBudget.t_tick_str` tick; full admission budget recorded separately | *Non-binding* \newline Defended by compact parameterized splines ($\beta < 100\text{ kB/s}$)                   | *Non-binding* \newline $P < 0.5\text{ W}$ (fixed-point constraint evaluation on MCU)                | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t \le 100\,\mu\text{s}$ (cycle-deterministic packet reception on MCU) | **BINDING** \newline Hardware boundary: private bus, separate oscillator, isolated held-up rail |
| **$\mathcal{H}_5$: Enforcer $\to$ Actuator** *(Body)*       | **BINDING** \newline $\tau \le 1.0\text{ ms}$ (servo interval $1.0\text{ ms}$; PWM loop $50\,\mu\text{s}$)                                                                                                                                                                     | *Non-binding* \newline $\beta \approx 1\text{--}5\text{ Mbps}$ (cyclic packets over deterministic command bus) | **BINDING** \newline $I^2 R$ copper winding dissipation, MOSFET switching losses                    | **BINDING** \newline $\sigma_t < 10\,\mu\text{s}$ (hard real-time PWM phase alignment & FOC)       | **BINDING** \newline Galvanic isolation, out-of-band analog E-stops, STO circuits               |

: **Handoffs-by-limits synthesis grid**: A five-by-five matrix mapping five canonical signal handoffs ($\mathcal{H}_1\text{--}\mathcal{H}_5$) across the Boundary (@sec-boundary-machine-model), Brain (@sec-brain), Body (@sec-body), and Nervous System (@sec-nervous) against five physical limits ($\tau, \beta, \mathcal{E}, \sigma_t, \mathcal{F}$). Cells marked *BINDING* are the budgets that drive selection; *Non-binding* means the scenario budget meets that dimension with margin. These illustrative allocations organize the timing and isolation evidence still required; a non-binding cell is not a qualification verdict. {#tbl-04-synthesis-grid tbl-colwidths="[16,16,18,18,16,16]"}

To ensure these budgets survive the lifecycle of the machine, every boundary condition in the grid is recorded as part of the machine's Transport Budget handoff record, the verifiable contract between hardware designers, systems engineers, and model developers. Each entry carries the six elements of a limit record (@sec-body-measuring-limits) and adds the fields that locate the limit at a handoff and say what kind of bound it is (@tbl-04-schema-notebook).

| Field Name               | Physical SI Units                                                | Structural Invariant & Description                                                                                                            |
|:-------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| `signal_id`              | dimensionless                                                    | Unique alphanumeric identifier (e.g. `SIG_VIO_01`, `SIG_TRQ_AX1`).                                                                            |
| `source_subsystem`       | dimensionless                                                    | Originating hardware or software module (`Camera_SerDes`, `Planner_VLA`).                                                                     |
| `destination_subsystem`  | dimensionless                                                    | Receiving hardware or software module (`State_Estimator`, `Safety_MCU`).                                                                      |
| `handoff`                | dimensionless                                                    | The handoff the signal crosses ($\mathcal{H}_1$ to $\mathcal{H}_5$).                                                                          |
| `physical_dimension`     | dimensionless                                                    | Target limit category ($\tau$, $\beta$, $\mathcal{E}$, $\sigma_t$, $\mathcal{F}$).                                                            |
| `value`                  | SI units ($\text{ms}$, $\text{MB/s}$, $\text{W}$, $\mu\text{s}$) | Allocated budget, or the measured distribution it is checked against; for $\mathcal{H}_4$, the chunk lease derived from the stopping budget.  |
| `conditions`             | as recorded                                                      | Payload, temperature, supply voltage, firmware build, and concurrent workload under which the value holds; the value lapses when they change. |
| `uncertainty`            | same as `value`                                                  | Error bound of the instrument or model that produced the value.                                                                               |
| `margin`                 | same as `value`                                                  | Engineering margin between the operating target and the breakdown threshold.                                                                  |
| `detector`               | dimensionless                                                    | Runtime monitor that catches an excursion (for example, a lease timer, a rail-voltage monitor, or a phase-current sensor).                    |
| `provenance`             | dimensionless                                                    | Source of the value, including its evidence category (measured, derived, datasheet, or illustrative).                                         |
| `bound_kind`             | dimensionless                                                    | `requirement`, `proven bound`, or `measured distribution`; only a proven bound may stand in for a worst case.                                 |
| `clock_domain`           | dimensionless                                                    | Clock on which every time-valued field is expressed; a handoff that feeds the permission path uses the safety microcontroller's clock.        |
| `verification_timestamp` | UTC timestamp                                                    | Date of bench falsification and sign-off; a log field, never an input to an age test.                                                         |

: **Conceptual fields of the handoff record**: The six limit-record elements of @sec-body-measuring-limits, extended with the handoff, bound kind, and clock domain that locate a limit in the machine and state what evidence supports it. {#tbl-04-schema-notebook tbl-colwidths="[22,24,54]"}

### Coupled budget synthesis for machine anatomy {#sec-nervous-coupled-budget}

The individual physical limits established across Part I do not operate in isolation: stopping distance, cognitive inference latency, memory bandwidth streaming, and deterministic command bus schedules converge into a single coupled timing equation. By linking the distance budget of the Body with the compute throughput of the Brain, the Nervous System establishes the allowable operational envelope for the entire embodied machine.

```{python}
#| label: calc-nervous-coupled-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ PART I COUPLED BUDGET: DISTANCE -> LEASE -> SUPPLY -> LEASE RULE (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @sec-nervous-coupled-budget.
# │ Goal:    Join Ch2's distance terms, this chapter's lease, and Ch3's supply
# │          rates into the lease rule for the running machine.
# │ Show:    ceiling 258.3 ms; running total 835.5 mm; intent sweep 98.0 ms,
# │          intent 2 Hz / 336 ms computed (INT4 sweep 24.5 ms); chunk sweep
# │          1.12 ms, 20 Hz / 40 ms;
# │          50 + 5 = 55 ms < 60 ms lease; upper limit 236.3 ms less age.
# │ How:     ceiling and running total read from MachineLeaseBudget;
# │          calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization on RM / AISLE; the 5 ms renewal jitter is a scenario assumption.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_latency, fmt_frequency, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class PartOneCoupledBudget:
    """The chunk lease as the meeting point of Part I's distance, timing, and supply budgets."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative
    t_act = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate  # category: chosen
    t_intent = RM.intent_inference_latency  # category: derived (prefill plus decode, @sec-brain-memory-wall)
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate  # category: chosen
    t_chunk = RM.chunk_inference_latency  # category: illustrative (P99, incl. vision)
    t_renewal_jitter = MachineLeaseBudget.t_renewal_jitter  # category: chosen (from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    t_ceiling = MachineLeaseBudget.t_ceiling  # from calc-nervous-machine-lease-budget
    running_total = MachineLeaseBudget.running_total  # one source for the stopping budget

    intent_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=RM.intent_weight_memory,  # deployed INT4 weights
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)
    chunk_sweep = calc_action_chunk_streaming_amortization(
        model_weight_memory=memory_from_params(RM.chunk_model.parameters, BYTES_FP16 / param),
        memory_bandwidth=RM.brain_soc.memory.bandwidth,
        chunk_horizon=RM.chunk_horizon,
        bus_efficiency=RM.dram_efficiency,
    )["t_stream"].to(millisecond)

    t_chunk_period = (1 / f_chunk).to(millisecond)
    t_renewal_need = (t_chunk_period + t_renewal_jitter).to(millisecond)  # lease lower limit
    t_lease_upper = (t_ceiling - t_tick - t_bus - t_act).to(millisecond)  # before observation age
    mm_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(t_ceiling.magnitude - 258.333) < 5e-3, f"Pre-brake ceiling drifted: {t_ceiling}")
    check(abs(running_total.magnitude - 835.5) < 1e-6, f"Running total drifted: {running_total}")
    # 2026-09-28 (M2): deployed INT4 intent weights; ACT corrected to about 80M parameters.
    check(abs(intent_sweep.magnitude - 24.51) < 5e-3, f"Intent weight sweep drifted: {intent_sweep}")
    check(abs(chunk_sweep.magnitude - 1.1204) < 5e-4, f"Chunk weight sweep drifted: {chunk_sweep}")
    check(abs(f_chunk.to(hertz).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk rate drifted: {f_chunk}")
    check(abs(f_intent.to(hertz).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, f"Intent rate drifted: {f_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk.to(millisecond).magnitude - 40.0) < 1e-9, f"Chunk inference latency drifted: {t_chunk}")
    check(abs(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude - 335.61) < 5e-3, f"Intent inference latency drifted: {t_intent}")
    check(abs(t_chunk_period.magnitude - 50.0) < 1e-6, f"Chunk period drifted: {t_chunk_period}")
    check(t_intent > t_lease, "The intent model must be unable to renew a chunk lease")
    check(t_chunk < t_chunk_period, "Chunk inference must finish within the chunk period")
    check(abs(t_renewal_need.magnitude - 55.0) < 1e-6, f"Lease lower limit drifted: {t_renewal_need}")
    check(t_renewal_need < t_lease, "Lease rule: chunk period plus jitter must be shorter than the lease")
    check(abs(t_lease_upper.magnitude - 236.333) < 5e-3, f"Lease upper limit (before age) drifted: {t_lease_upper}")
    check(t_lease <= t_lease_upper - AISLE.perception_age, "Lease rule: lease must fit the ceiling after tick, bus, onset, and age")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Format & Export) ────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    t_ceiling_str = fmt_latency(t_ceiling, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    running_total_str = fmt_length(running_total, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    intent_sweep_str = fmt_latency(intent_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_intent_str = fmt_latency(round(t_intent.to(millisecond).magnitude) * millisecond, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    f_intent_str = fmt_frequency(f_intent, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    chunk_sweep_str = fmt_latency(chunk_sweep, unit=millisecond, precision=2)
    f_chunk_str = fmt_frequency(f_chunk, unit=hertz, precision=0)
    t_chunk_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_chunk_period_str = fmt_latency(t_chunk_period, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_jitter_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_jitter, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_renewal_need_str = fmt_latency(t_renewal_need, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_upper_str = fmt_latency(t_lease_upper, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    mm_per_ms_str = fmt_length(mm_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
```

The three chapters of Part I each set terms of one budget, and the chunk lease is where they meet. @Sec-body-kinetic-momentum fixed the distance side. At its `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.v_str` drive limit the loaded machine must stop inside the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance at a rack end, and the braking term and the fixed overheads leave `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` for everything that happens before braking force begins. @Sec-nervous-cadences spent part of that time. A proposer that stalls keeps its authority for one lease, the stop reaches the drives one tick and one bus cycle later, and the stopping budget stands at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.running_total_str`.

The lease cannot be made as short as the budget would like, because a proposer must renew it. @Sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline established what each learned proposer can supply. The intent model's INT4 weights take `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.intent_sweep_str` to stream from memory once, but a full inference, a compute-bound prefill followed by bandwidth-bound decode sweeps, takes `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_intent_str`, so at `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_intent_str` it cannot renew a proposal every few tens of milliseconds. The chunk policy's weights stream in `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.chunk_sweep_str`, and its selected `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.f_chunk_str` cadence calls for a fresh chunk every `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_period_str`. Its illustrative `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_chunk_str` P99 inference time makes that cadence a plausible supply target, not a guaranteed renewal bound. Late or missing renewals remain the permission path's responsibility.

These facts fix the **lease rule**\index{Chunk lease!lease rule} for this machine. For continuous tracking, the lease must outlast the chosen successful-admission interval plus its variation allowance, which together set the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_renewal_need_str` floor of \ref{nbk-nervous-watchdog-stopping-lease}. It must also fit inside the pre-brake ceiling once the tick, the bus cycle, and brake onset are reserved, which leaves `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_upper_str` less the evidence age at admission. The capture-to-dispatch age developed in @sec-perception is only part of that subtraction; dispatch-to-admission work remains an unclosed allowance in this calculation. The chosen `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_str` sits just above the renewal target, because every millisecond of lease costs `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.mm_per_ms_str` at the drive limit. It remains a candidate allocation until the complete capture-to-admission age and later response terms fit. Increasing the lease to hide admission delays would spend further clearance rather than close that missing budget.

Each chunk carries the base's velocity and the arm's joint targets together, so the selected architecture uses one candidate lease for both bodies. Each body must have a feasible state-matched response when that lease lapses. The base's `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_ceiling_str` pre-brake ceiling constrains the allocation here; it does not establish that the arm has more margin. The illustrative arm calculation in @sec-planning-handoff checks response travel and stopping against its own clearance. Qualifying the shared lease requires both bodies' timing, evidence, current state, and fallback limits to hold. The arm's evidence horizon bounds a different lease, the intent lease, which limits how long an admitted goal from the intent model stays valid, and the intent model's slower targets expire under it (@sec-intent-lease).

The $\mathcal{H}_4$ row of @tbl-04-synthesis-grid is this chapter's Transport Budget handoff record filled in, combining the Limit Record (@sec-body) with the proposer limits from @sec-brain. Its value is the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.t_lease_str` chunk lease handed from the chunk policy to the permission path, a `requirement` proposed for the `{python} PartOneCoupledBudget.v_str` drive limit, loaded, on a dry floor, at the admission-renewal target above; its final margin remains unresolved until evidence age through admission and the remaining stop terms are bounded, and its detector is the lease timer on the safety microcontroller, counted on that processor's own clock.
